## The idea

The [hold gate](hold-gate.qmd) and the [certificate over a whole box of
poses](certificate.qmd) certify that the block *can be held* at every pose
along a plan. A **funnel**
certifies the motion itself:

- **Entry set.** A box of states the edge may start from: pose, velocity,
  contact offsets, and μ<sub>disk</sub> ∈ [0.3, 0.5].
- **Law and tube.** A feedback law and a tube around its nominal motion.
- **Certificate.** For every state in the entry set and every friction in
  the band, the motion stays in the tube, the contact forces stay inside
  their cones and above a derived floor, the motor stays in its box, and the
  edge ends inside the next edge's entry set.
- **Check.** The certified edge is executed in MJX from measured states, and
  the measured coverage is reported at 95/95.

Edges whose sets compose this way form a chain that is certified end to end.
The block no longer has to be held at every instant, so rolls, landings in
motion and coasting become plannable edges.

## Track C: a chain with a landing in motion

The chain tips the block, pivots it on the step corner, breaks and remakes
contact, rolls it over the corner, pushes it so that it lands on the platform
in motion, transports it into the lift goal, stops it there and lets go.
Every segment below is certified for every state of its entry set and every
disk friction in [0.3, 0.5]; the "utilization" is the certificate's smallest
remaining margin as a fraction of its capacity, so **higher is safer**.

::: {.table-responsive}

| Piece | Certificate | Utilization | MJX from real entry states |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tip (held departure, tip funnel) | yes | 0.47 | — |
| Pivot to 59.00° (law switch at 23°) | yes | 0.225 | 992 / 992 |
| Stop at 59.00° | yes, derived force floor | rest 58.996–59.052° | — |
| Gentle break, then make(m<sub>z</sub>) | yes (one certificate) | — | 300 / 300 |
| Break(g<sub>v</sub>) into the roll | yes | 0.545 | 687 / 687 |
| Roll over the corner at 1°/s, from the 62° junction | yes | 0.376 | 765 / 765 |
| Push, 0.1116 N, on 16 sub-boxes of the roll's exit | yes | 0.686 | — |
| **Landing impact window** | **yes, zonotope cover** | 310,372 pieces, 0 uncertified | — |
| **Rest after the impact** | **yes, energy (dissipation) inequality** | 16,384 / 16,384 units | every landing comes to rest |
| Transport through the support switch, wide (β 0.25), from the certified departure | yes, zonotope tube | 0.247 | 731 / 731 held-out |
| **Goal stop** (held force c<sub>n</sub> 0.15 N) | **yes**, through the two-model rest | — | 1536 / 1536 end inside its rest set |
| **Release**, break(m<sub>z</sub>) | **yes**, passive braking ≥ 1.94 m/s² | — | 1536 / 1536 settle inside the rigid rest set |
| Block at rest after the release | **yes**, passive hold, every slip and tip excluded | — | 1536 / 1536 |

:::

In the chain's own count all **14 of 14 segments** are certified (the break
and the make are two) and all **16 of 16 junctions** between and inside them.
One quantity is not in the rigid reduction and is measured in MJX: the disk's
clearance after it lifts off the block in the release.

**How the edges compose.** A junction composes when the certified exit of one
edge lies inside the certified entry of the next; sets measured in simulation
only validate coverage. An automatic check reads every certificate's exported
sets and tests each junction, and every one passes on certified sets:

- the ten junctions from the block at rest through the impact window;
- into the rest after the impact: the energy certificate's units start from
  the impact window's certified hand-off set;
- out of that rest into the transport: the departure from the certified rest
  set, grown by the hold creep, is certified on 4 slices of the disk's place
  k, and the wide transport funnel is re-verified from that departure set;
- from the transport into the goal stop, which brakes at 0.15 N, and from the
  goal stop into the release;
- from the release into the block at rest: the release's passive braking ends
  in its own passive hold, the same pattern as the impact window ending in
  the post-impact rest.

**Executed end to end.** 768 rollouts at each end of the friction band. Each
is one continuous MuJoCo/MJX simulation from the block at rest to the wide
transport's exit (its commands bitwise equal to the certified wide law), and a
second MJX run carries every rollout on through the goal stop and the release;
every law switches at its certified hand-off.
The block reaches the lift goal, released and at rest, in **1536 of 1536**
(Clopper–Pearson 95% [0.9976, 1]). Through the goal stop's hold, 1528 of 1536
stay inside its rest set; the other 8 dip at most 1.1 µm below it at the
first step, and all 1536 end inside it.

**Why the chain ends with a release.** A rigid model holds a pushed block
perfectly still, but MJX's contact is soft: under a held push its friction
lets the block creep, 18–25 µm/s at 0.15 N, for as long as the push lasts.
The certified way to end a plan is therefore to stop pushing. Once the block
has stopped, the disk breaks its contact (break(m<sub>z</sub>)), and the block
rests on the platform with no disk force at all. That rest is certified: the
platform's friction brakes any remaining slide at no less than 1.94 m/s², and
every slip and tip is excluded. In MJX all 1536 rollouts settle inside the
rigid rest set; through the disk's retraction the block moves at most 24 µm
and tilts at most 0.0055°.

**The rest after the landing impact.** The rest is certified by a dissipation
(energy) inequality on all 16,384 post-impact units: friction at the platform
and at the disk dissipates the kinetic energy faster than the hold force
supplies it, which bounds how far the block slides and how far the disk slips
on its face ([Background: dissipation certificates](passivity-certificates.qmd)).
The certified rest set has x<sub>B</sub> ∈ [0.475, 3.666] mm and
k<sub>m<sub>z</sub></sub> ∈ [−9.608, +0.104] mm; per unit, the block slides
at most 1.70 mm and k shifts at most 1.53 mm.

**A barrier on the wide transport.** A discrete-time barrier on the support
load is verified over the wide transport through the support switch with a
decay rate γ* = 0.0048 per step and no subdivision
([Background: control barrier functions](control-barrier-functions.qmd)).

*Record:* a second variant of the chain uses a narrower transport (to
62.571 mm, utilization 0.208) and a goal stop at 0.094 N without a release;
in it 11 of 12 segments are certified and the rest after the impact is
counted as measured.

## The landing impact, certified with zonotopes

Every other piece above is certified by **interval arithmetic**
([Background: interval arithmetic](interval-arithmetic.qmd)). Around the
landing impact that fails: intervals store only axis-aligned boxes, every step
shears and rotates the set, and re-wrapping it adds empty corners that
compound (the wrapping effect). Splitting the boxes finely enough would have
needed on the order of 2<sup>36</sup> pieces.

Carried as a **zonotope**, the set keeps the correlations a box throws away.
Over the whole landing set the cover needs **310,372 pieces, all certified,
none uncertified**, computed in about seven hours on two clusters. Sampled
trajectories (1.13 million step checks) and exact rational solves of the
contact system (253,000) found no escape from the certified sets. The thinnest
certified margin lies in a contact case that no sampled trajectory takes: an
over-approximation, sound as it stands.

## A set-based route: zonotopes

*Background: [zonotope propagation](zonotopes.qmd) derives the operations
below, with proofs, and maps each funnel check onto them.*

The remedy is to certify a **set shape** that a step maps without
re-wrapping. A zonotope is

  **c + G · [−1, 1]<sup>k</sup>**,

a centre plus a linear image of a cube.

- **A linear step maps it exactly.** It just multiplies G. A nonlinear step
  is linearized, its Jacobian multiplies G, and only the small remainder is
  boxed. In validated integration this is Lohner's method, the first-order
  Taylor form.
- **Checks stay cheap.** The minimum of a linear quantity a·x over the
  zonotope is a·c − Σ|a·G|. Force floors and friction cones cost about what
  they cost on boxes.
- **General polytopes don't scale.** Their face and vertex counts grow
  exponentially with the dimension, and a nonlinear map does not map a
  polytope to a polytope.
- **The hard part is the contact switch.** At impact, part of the set is
  already in contact and part is not. The set has to be split along the
  contact guard and each part followed in its own mode. A **hybrid
  zonotope**, a union of constrained zonotopes indexed by binary factors,
  represents exactly such a mode-branched set
  ([Bird, Pangborn, Jain and Koeln, *Automatica* 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.14831);
  for nonlinear steps,
  [Siefert et al., ACC 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.09902)).

**The method in this chain.** The funnel certifier runs the zonotope set type
on every edge, the impact window included, and the edges certified both ways
hold with zonotope margins equal to or above their interval margins. Interval arithmetic stays the
rigorous subroutine for remainder bounds, implicit contact solves and
rounding ([Background: intervals and zonotopes together](intervals-and-zonotopes.qmd)).

::: {.callout-note title="Where this leads"}
With the impact window certified, set-based certificates for contact-rich
funnels deserve to be pursued well beyond this chain.

Justin Koeln and Justin Ruths at UT Dallas work on exactly these set
representations: hybrid zonotopes for reachability of mixed logical
dynamical systems, and the zonoLAB toolbox
([arXiv 2310.15426](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.15426)). That line would be a
natural collaboration.
:::
